title: Nvidia Bulls Face a Concentration Problem as Custom AI Chips Gain Ground
excerpt: Three customers account for more than half of Nvidia's quarterly revenue, and the push toward in-house silicon by hyperscalers is testing investor confidence in the chip giant's premium valuation.
body:
• Three customers accounted for 21%, 17%, and 16% of Nvidia's last quarter revenue — over half from just three buyers
  • Nvidia's stock has underperformed the broader semiconductor index in 2026 despite 85% year-over-year revenue growth
  • Hyperscalers like Meta and Google are investing heavily in custom AI chips, threatening Nvidia's GPU dominance
  • Nvidia is diversifying into CPUs with its Vera architecture, guiding for 0 billion in CPU sales by fiscal year-end

The Numbers Look Great. The Risk Is Underneath.

Nvidia posted fiscal first-quarter revenue of 1.6 billion, up 85% year over year, with data-center sales surging 92% to 5.2 billion. CEO Jensen Huang declared that "agentic AI has arrived." By most financial measures, the company continues to dominate the AI infrastructure buildout.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=ZO0TgDCV8ow

But for investors, there is a growing disconnect between Nvidia's headline numbers and its stock performance. Shares have gained only about 7% in 2026, lagging the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index, which is up 58% over the same period. At a market capitalization near .5 trillion, the stock trades at roughly 34 times earnings — its cheapest forward multiple in about two years, according to Motley Fool analysis.

The Concentration Bear Case

Nvidia's latest 10-Q filing reveals that three customers accounted for 21%, 17%, and 16% of last quarter's sales. That kind of customer concentration is not new for chipmakers, but with the stock near a trillion valuation, it carries outsized risk.

Over 90% of Nvidia's revenue comes from data-center sales, leaving little margin for error. The bear case centers on what happens when those same top customers — the hyperscalers building the world's largest AI data centers — start designing their own silicon.

Meta Platforms is going big on in-house chip development, according to recent reports. Google has been running its Tensor Processing Units for years. Amazon Web Services has its Trainium and Inferentia chips. The risk is not that these replace Nvidia's GPUs overnight, but that they gradually erode margins at the high end of the market.

"Expectations have gotten to be almost impossible to beat for these companies."

— Zachary Hill, Horizon Investments

Nvidia's Response: Vera and Beyond

Nvidia is not standing still. The company is pushing aggressively into CPUs, networking, systems, and software. Its Vera CPU architecture has drawn early interest, with Perplexity announcing it will use the chip. Nate Kupp, a vice president at Perplexity, called Vera "a dead-on fit" after tests showed Nvidia's CPU ran AI agent coding about 1.5 times faster than standard chips, according to Reuters.

Nvidia is guiding for 0 billion in Vera CPU sales by fiscal year-end. The company also authorized 0 billion in stock buybacks on top of the 0.2 billion it repurchased last quarter, giving it a financial cushion against multiple compression.

Meanwhile, reports that China's DeepSeek is developing its own inference chip add another dimension. Richard Windsor at Radio Free Mobile told Reuters: "Nvidia is at zero in China and staying there." The direct damage from China is capped, but if inference chips go custom sooner than bulls expect, it could accelerate the margin pressure.

What Investors Are Watching

Nvidia's stock sits just above its 200-day moving average, a level that technical traders watch closely. As long as it holds above that mark, the stock is viewed as pressured but structurally sound. A break below would signal that the market is pricing in the risk that AI growth continues but Nvidia's share of it shrinks.

Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin chip architecture has witnessed unprecedented demand, and the company's backlog is estimated at several hundred billion dollars. Wall Street consensus remains a Strong Buy, with an average price target implying meaningful upside. But the gap between Nvidia's growth story and its stock performance in 2026 suggests investors are no longer willing to pay the same premium for dominance that may not last.
